starter-dam: The first, low embankment of a tailings dam, built of soil or rock before any tailings arrive. Later raises are built on it, beside it or beyond it as the deposit grows.
downstream-raise: Raising a tailings dam by building each new lift over the outer slope of the last, so the crest steps away from the pond. Every raise rests on compacted fill or natural ground, and a core and drains can be carried up with it; it takes the most fill.
centreline-raise: Raising a tailings dam straight up: each lift sits on the crest of the last, spills down the outer slope, and puts a small wedge on the top of the beach, which must be sandy, drained and compacted.
modified-centreline: A way of raising a tailings dam between centreline and upstream: each raise steps its crest a little toward the pond, so more of it rests on the beach, and the core leans upstream, supported on that side by a zone of tailings.
cyclone-sand: The coarse part of the tailings, separated from the fines and most of the water by spinning the slurry in a hydrocyclone. It drains freely and can be compacted, so it is used to build the walls of tailings dams.
hydraulic-fill: Soil washed into place as a slurry and left to settle. It was a common way to build earth dams early in the twentieth century; it leaves the fill loose and saturated unless it is compacted afterwards.
rate-of-rise: How many metres a year the surface of a tailings deposit climbs: the volume deposited each year divided by the area it covers. Too fast, and the water in the tailings cannot drain away before the next metre arrives.

entry: Raising a tailings dam by building each new dyke on the tailings beach, so the crest steps toward the pond. It takes the least fill, and it rests on loose, saturated tailings that can liquefy; Chile and Brazil prohibit it.

Liquefaction with no earthquake. Loose, saturated soil pushed slowly, by a new load, a steepening slope, creep or rising water, tries to pack tighter; the water cannot leave in time, takes the load, and the soil flows.
